positioning.text: SenDISA, an AI engine that fuses video, ANPR, GPS, LiDAR and acoustic data into court-grade evidence and automated workflows for government. Sold as a detection and intelligence layer that runs on cameras a city already owns.

target_customers.text: 27 Smart City customers in North America at FY26 close, reached largely through channel partners rather than a direct field team.
US and Canadian cities: Pittsburgh Parking Authority, Toronto Exhibition Place, Kitchener, Mississauga, Medford, Las Vegas, Calgary and Montreal.

key_capabilities.text: Runs on the city's existing camera estate and VMS rather than a proprietary camera fleet, which removes the day-one hardware bill.
One engine spans parking and curb, road defects (40-plus types with severity ratings), asset and signage cataloguing, and worksite safety from the same patrol pass.
Human-in-the-loop by design: the AI detects and evidences, a trained officer reviews every event and makes every enforcement decision.
Open REST APIs and webhooks into existing ERP, GIS, asset, ticketing, payment and permit systems, with 200-plus technology partners.

pricing_summary.text: No public price list. Sold as an annual subscription with no upfront capital expenditure and multi-year payment plans. Disclosed contract values imply roughly A$1 per head of population per year in large cities: Calgary at A$1.9M in year one and A$4.6M over five years.

recent_changes.text: FY26: ARR reached A$11.7M, up 17%; cash receipts a record A$16.0M; EBITDA A$2.0M, up 23.6%; customer churn 5.6%. Revenue finished only slightly ahead of the prior year as NVIDIA hardware supply issues pushed projects into FY27.

FY26 added five North American city contracts - Pittsburgh Parking Authority, Toronto Exhibition Place, Birmingham, Kitchener and Mississauga - taking the North American Smart City base to 27, with four already live.
FY26 multi-year renewals at Las Vegas, Cairns, Ipswich and Newcastle.
FY25: revenue A$15.4M, up 27%, and a first net profit of about A$450k after a A$3.6M loss in FY24.

review_weaknesses.text: Market capitalisation sits around A$25M in mid-2026, against Genetec's 2,100-plus employees and Arrive's 90-country footprint. Expect vendor-viability questions in any large US procurement.
Churn was 5.6% in FY26, which contradicts the long-running investor narrative of negligible churn.

North American delivery runs largely through channel partners such as gtechna rather than a direct field team. SenSen does contract directly in some markets - Calgary and Montreal were direct tender wins - so describe the model as mixed, never as 'we contract directly'.

quotes.quote: Annualised recurring revenue grew to $11.7 million, up 17% on the prior year, cash receipts reached a record $16.0 million and customer churn was just 5.6%.

Global supply-chain disruptions, particularly around the NVIDIA-based hardware used in many of our deployments, combined with more cautious customer spending, delayed several projects in Singapore and Australia moving some upfront revenue that we had expected in FY26 into FY27.

positioning.text: The global leader in enterprise physical security software by market share. Security Center unifies video, access control, ALPR, intrusion and communications, and AutoVu is its ALPR family for parking enforcement and vehicle investigation. Sold exclusively through accredited channel partners.

target_customers.text: 42,500-plus customers across 159 countries, served through accredited channel partners and about 2,500 integrators.
US parking and campus enforcement: City of Fort Lauderdale and Cornell University are among the published AutoVu customers.
Key markets are public safety, government, education, healthcare, retail, banking, energy and transportation. Parking is one application of a broader security platform.

key_capabilities.text: AutoVu mobile and fixed ALPR enforces permits, time limits, pay-by-plate and scofflaw lists in a single patrol pass, using SharpX cameras on enforcement vehicles.

AutoVu Cloudrunner, its vehicle-centric investigation system, captures plate, colour, type, make and model and driving behaviours regardless of time of day or weather, and integrates with third-party alerting platforms such as SaferWatch.
AutoVu Free-Flow tracks occupancy and violations in gateless lots as vehicles enter and exit.
AutoVu Managed Services hosts the ALPR system in the cloud, removing installation and maintenance overhead.
Unified security: body-worn devices, video, access control and intercom in one platform, which keeps operator training low and covers officer safety.
Open architecture with an SDK and partner programmes, positioned explicitly to help customers scale without vendor lock-in.

pricing_summary.text: No public pricing: Genetec sells only through accredited channel partners, so price is quoted per project by a reseller. Its best-known commercial proof point is payback rather than price, with Fort Lauderdale recouping its ALPR investment in about two months - though that case study is undated and its image metadata dates to 2015.

recent_changes.text: August 2026: Omdia and Novaira Insights ranked Genetec the global market leader in video management software. Omdia put its 2025 growth at 20% against a market growing 13.3%, and Novaira ranked it number one in the Americas for the fifteenth consecutive year.
March 2026: added access control capabilities to Security Center SaaS, including a front desk experience, expanded intrusion panel support and optional biometrics.
February 2026: told its Global Press Summit it works with about 2,500 integrators as channel partners, and published a State of Physical Security Report drawing on 7,300 respondents.

Its current corporate fact sheet lists 2,300-plus employees worldwide and 42,500-plus clients across 159 countries. Genetec's own about page still says 2,200-plus, so quote the fact sheet figure and expect small variations in their material.
May 2025: integrated AutoVu Cloudrunner with the SaferWatch alerting platform for public safety agencies, developed with the Hawaii Department of Law Enforcement.

review_weaknesses.text: Parking is one module of a security platform, not the product. AutoVu sits inside Security Center, so a parking team buys into a wider security estate and its upgrade cycle.

Channel-only distribution: Genetec serves customers exclusively through accredited partners and about 2,500 integrators, so there is no direct price and the implementation relationship sits with a reseller whose capability varies by region.
No published road-condition, asset-register or kerb-inventory capability, so a city wanting more than enforcement and vehicle investigation from the same patrol needs a second system.
The headline US parking reference, Fort Lauderdale, is an undated case study whose embedded image metadata dates to 2015, and it predates the current AutoVu line-up.
Buyers on review sites repeatedly flag a steep learning curve and setup complexity for the platform.

hiring_signals.text: Over 100 roles open at the time of its July 2025 expansion announcement, with headcount up 65% since 2020.

quotes.quote: Genetec grew 20% against the 13.3% growth in the video software and VSaaS market, according to the latest Omdia research.
Headquartered in Montreal, Canada, Genetec serves its 42,500+ customers via an extensive network of accredited channel partners and consultants in over 159 countries.

positioning.text: A global mobility platform that, since completing the Passport acquisition on 1 October 2026, now sells parking enforcement in North America as well as payments. Arrive is EasyPark Group renamed in June 2025, parent of ParkMobile, EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo and Parkopedia, and Passport adds citation issuance, digital permits and LPR-based enforcement across more than 800 North American cities and operators.

target_customers.text: Passport is used by more than 800 North American cities and parking operators for paid parking, enforcement and payment infrastructure; its own literature cites nearly 1,000 clients worldwide.
ParkMobile is the group's long-standing North American payments brand, available in over 700 US cities.
Globally, more than 20,000 cities across 90 countries through EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo, Parkopedia and Yellowbrick.

key_capabilities.text: Passport enforcement is an end-to-end citation platform: LPR and digital chalking in the field, citation issuance in under a minute, photo evidence, scofflaw management, adjudication and appeals, DMV lookup, letter generation and revenue recovery.
LPR cameras mount on enforcement vehicles with an in-car tablet, or officers use handheld cameras; Passport states its LPR integrations let officers scan up to 4,000 plates a day.
Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware rather than supplying its own cameras - its own wording is 'integrate with various LPR technologies'.
Digital permits tied to licence plates, removing hang tags and decals, with permit and enforcement data connected in one platform.
Digital parking payments at scale through ParkMobile, EasyPark, RingGo and Yellowbrick, owned outright rather than integrated.
Flowbird pay stations and smart ticketing, and Parkopedia in-dash data, payments and indoor navigation.

pricing_summary.text: No published municipal pricing for either the payments or the enforcement products. Consumer transaction pricing is public through the apps; city and operator contracts are not disclosed.

recent_changes.text: 1 October 2026: completed the acquisition of Passport, adding parking compliance, citation issuance and LPR-based enforcement across 800-plus North American cities and operators. Backed by Vitruvian Partners, Verdane and Searchlight Capital Partners.
8 October 2026: the US Department of Justice Antitrust Division closed its investigation into the deal after issuing Second Requests, concluding a substantial reduction in competition was unlikely.
4 March 2026: announced the intent to acquire Passport, explicitly to unify enforcement technology, paid parking and payment infrastructure into one platform.

12 June 2025: EasyPark Group renamed itself Arrive, after buying the rights to the name from Flash, which had held them since its 2021 merger with the earlier Arrive Mobility (ParkWhiz and BestParking).
January and February 2025: completed the acquisitions of Flowbird Group and Parkopedia.

review_weaknesses.text: Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware rather than supplying its own cameras, so the detection layer in an Arrive enforcement deal belongs to someone else.

On the payments side, the US Department of Justice recorded that Passport 'has declined to bid for or has lost some recent notable' mobile parking payment contracts. That is an independent read on the payments business specifically, not on enforcement.

evidence.text: Passport has declined to bid for or has lost some recent notable MPP contracts.

review_weaknesses.text: Four major changes inside twenty months: Flowbird (January 2025), Parkopedia (February 2025), the group rebrand (June 2025) and Passport (completed October 2026). Arrive itself says organisational structure updates 'will follow in the coming months'.

evidence.text: updates on our organizational structure will follow in the coming months

review_weaknesses.text: No published road-condition, asset-register or kerb-inventory capability, so a city wanting more than enforcement from the same patrol still needs a second system.
Two different US parking companies have traded as Arrive: Flash still operates the former Arrive Mobility assets, ParkWhiz and BestParking. Expect confusion in procurement records.

quotes.quote: Until now, Arrive has lacked a substantial compliance and enforcement offering in North America, a gap that Passport nicely fills.
Passport has declined to bid for or has lost some recent notable MPP contracts.

battlecards.overview: A 2,300-person unified physical security platform company, ranked number one worldwide in video management software, whose AutoVu ALPR family is a direct and well-proven competitor for US municipal parking enforcement. Sold only through accredited channel partners.
battlecards.tldr: We win when the city wants more than enforcement out of the patrol and a sensor-agnostic layer over feeds it already runs. We lose when the buyer is a security department standardising on one platform, or wants the measured market leader behind the signature.
battlecards.quick_dismiss: Genetec is the strongest competitor in this set and the market-share leader in video management. The distinction is scope, not scale: AutoVu is ALPR and vehicle investigation inside a security platform. SenDISA is a sensor-agnostic city intelligence engine that also returns road and asset condition from the same drive. Ask what the patrol should deliver in three years.

where_we_win.headline: One patrol pass, several departments
where_we_win.detail: The same drive returns 40-plus road defect types with severity ratings, a versioned asset and signage register, and worksite safety detection. Genetec publishes no road-condition or asset-register capability, so that is a second system and a second contract.

where_we_win.headline: Sensor-agnostic fusion, not an ALPR product
where_we_win.detail: SenDISA fuses video, ANPR, GPS, LiDAR and acoustic data and connects to CCTV, GIS, sensor and traffic feeds the city already runs. AutoVu is an ALPR family - excellent at plates and vehicle investigation, but scoped to vehicles rather than the whole street picture.

where_we_win.headline: The integration model is proven, not theoretical
where_we_win.detail: SenForce powers gtechna's Ticket-by-Mail, and SenSen's FY26 results name Pittsburgh Parking Authority and Kitchener among its new North American city contracts, with Medford presented jointly with gtechna. A city keeping its existing citation system is how much of our North American base is deployed.

where_we_win.headline: Calgary retendered openly and retained us
where_we_win.detail: A customer since 2016, Calgary issued an RFP in 2024 to replace its vehicle monitoring and enforcement technology and, after a global search, selected SenSen to continue: A$4.6M over five years with two further two-year options. The published sources do not name the other bidders, so claim the open retender and the renewal, not a head-to-head win over any particular vendor.

where_we_lose.headline: Market leadership, independently measured
where_we_lose.detail: Omdia and Novaira Insights rank Genetec number one worldwide in video management software, growing 20% in 2025 against a 13.3% market, and number one in the Americas for fifteen consecutive years. Against that, our market capitalisation is around A$25M.
where_we_lose.counter: Do not fight it on size. Move to the specific decision: what the patrol returns beyond citations, and whether the city wants a security platform or a city intelligence layer.

where_we_lose.headline: Published payback, not just outcomes
where_we_lose.detail: Fort Lauderdale booted over 600 scofflaw vehicles, collected over $200,000 in unpaid fines within eight months and recouped the system cost in about two months. (Fort Lauderdale case study is undated; its embedded image metadata dates to 2015, so treat the figures as roughly a decade old.) It is still a cleaner commercial story than we publish.
where_we_lose.counter: Match it with operational outcomes we can evidence, note the age of their reference, and offer a reference call rather than a case study.

where_we_lose.headline: One platform for security and parking
where_we_lose.detail: If the buyer also owns video surveillance, access control and intrusion, Security Center unifies all of it with one operator training burden. Parking alone rarely wins that argument.
where_we_lose.counter: Qualify early: if the economic buyer is the security department rather than parking or transport, this is their deal to lose. Partner rather than fight.

where_we_lose.headline: Vehicle investigation depth
where_we_lose.detail: AutoVu Cloudrunner captures plate, colour, type, make, model and driving behaviour for investigations, and integrates with public safety alerting platforms. That is a police-facing capability set we do not match.
where_we_lose.counter: Different buyer. Keep the conversation with parking, transport and public works rather than law enforcement.

where_we_lose.headline: Professional services and certification depth
where_we_lose.detail: Remote and on-site professional services, about 2,500 integrator partners, and technology and A&E consultant programmes. We publish none of that.
where_we_lose.counter: Lead with direct access to the people who build the product, and be honest that our North American delivery also runs through partners.

landmines.question: Can the same patrol tell us which signs are faded and which roads are failing, or is that a separate procurement?
landmines.why: No published road-condition or asset-register capability. It reframes the comparison from enforcement to what the drive returns.

landmines.question: Who holds the implementation contract - Genetec or the reseller - and what happens if we change reseller mid-term?
landmines.why: Genetec serves customers exclusively through accredited channel partners, so continuity of delivery sits with a third party.

landmines.question: If we are not standardising on one security platform, what are we paying for in Security Center that parking will never use?
landmines.why: AutoVu sits inside a unified security platform. A parking-only buyer should test how much of that estate they actually need.

landmines.question: What is the published deployment timeframe, and who commits to it contractually?
landmines.why: Genetec publishes no deployment timeframe; projects are scoped by the partner. We publish 2-4 weeks for vision and 6-8 weeks for asset management.

landmines.question: How recent is the reference you are being shown, and does it use the current product line-up?
landmines.why: The headline Fort Lauderdale parking reference is undated with 2015-era image metadata. Ask any vendor, including us, for a deployment from the last two years.

objections.objection: Genetec is a far bigger, safer company than you.
objections.response: True, and independently measured - they lead video management market share. If the decision is vendor size it is theirs. The decision we would put in front of you is scope: AutoVu reads plates and investigates vehicles; SenDISA also returns road condition, signage and asset data from the same drive. Calgary retendered openly in 2024 and kept us for up to nine years.

objections.objection: We already run Genetec Security Center for video and access control.
objections.response: Then keep it. We are a detection and intelligence layer, not a security platform, and we integrate through open REST APIs and webhooks into what you already run. The question is what the city wants read from the street: AutoVu reads plates and investigates vehicles, SenDISA also returns road condition, signage and asset data from the same pass.

objections.objection: Fort Lauderdale paid for its AutoVu system in two months. Can you show that?
objections.response: That is a strong number, though the case study is undated and its image metadata points to 2015, so it is worth asking for something recent. Ours is a different shape: no upfront capital expenditure, an annual subscription, and value that compounds because the same patrol feeds parking, road condition and asset data.

objections.objection: Our reseller has looked after us for years.
objections.response: Keep that relationship where it adds value, and in fairness our own North American delivery also runs largely through channel partners. The difference is that Genetec sells exclusively through partners, so ask what happens contractually if the reseller changes, and whether you can get a roadmap commitment from the vendor directly.

pricing_comparison.text: Neither vendor publishes a price list, but the models differ. Genetec is channel-only, so a city gets a reseller quote covering SharpX cameras, in-vehicle hardware and Security Center licensing; its best-known commercial proof is payback at Fort Lauderdale, an undated case study whose embedded image metadata dates to 2015. SenSen is an annual subscription with no upfront capital expenditure and multi-year payment plans, and disclosed contract values imply roughly A$1 per head of population per year in large cities - Calgary at A$1.9M in year one and A$4.6M over five.

proof_quotes.quote: Within the first eight months of installing its first AutoVu ALPR system, the City of Fort Lauderdale was able to boot over 600 scofflaw vehicles and collect over $200,000 in unpaid fines.
Headquartered in Montreal, Canada, Genetec serves its customers via an extensive network of certified channel partners and consultants in over 159 countries.
Works with your existing cameras and VMS systems with zero downtime during deployment. No infrastructure overhaul required.

battlecards.overview: Since completing the Passport acquisition on 1 October 2026, Arrive sells parking enforcement in North America as well as payments: citation issuance, digital permits and LPR-based enforcement across 800-plus cities and operators, on top of ParkMobile's 700-plus US cities.
battlecards.tldr: No longer a payments-only adjacency. Arrive now owns the citation back office across 800-plus North American cities - structurally the same layer as gtechna, our own channel partner. We win on the detection engine, which Passport does not build. We lose when a city wants payments, permits and enforcement on one contract.
battlecards.quick_dismiss: Arrive bought enforcement rather than building it. Passport is a strong citation and permit platform, but its own documentation says it integrates with various LPR technologies and relies on third-party LPR hardware. So the question in an Arrive deal is whose AI is actually detecting the violation, and what evidence standard it meets when a citation is challenged.

where_we_win.headline: The detection hardware is someone else's
where_we_win.detail: Passport's own product pages say it integrates with various LPR technologies and describe LPR camera hardware mounted on enforcement vehicles with an in-car tablet. That is an integration position rather than an owned detection stack - worth establishing whose engine is reading the plate, and on what evidence standard.

where_we_win.headline: More than enforcement from the same patrol
where_we_win.detail: SenDISA returns 40-plus road defect types with severity ratings, a versioned asset and signage register and worksite safety detection from the drive the city already runs. Arrive publishes no road-condition or asset-register capability across any of its brands.

where_we_win.headline: A government read on their payments position
where_we_win.detail: The DOJ's closing statement records that Passport has declined to bid for or lost some recent notable mobile parking payment contracts, and that viable alternatives exist. That is about the payments business, not detection, but it is an independent assessment of how the bundle is actually competing.

where_we_win.headline: Integration load at its peak
where_we_win.detail: Flowbird, Parkopedia, the group rebrand and now Passport - four major changes in twenty months, with Arrive itself saying organisational structure updates will follow in the coming months. A city signing a multi-year contract is signing into that.

where_we_lose.headline: They now own the citation back office we partner into
where_we_lose.detail: Passport covers citation issuance, permits, adjudication, DMV lookup and revenue recovery across 800-plus North American cities. That is structurally the same layer as gtechna, our own channel partner in North America. Where Arrive wins the back office, our route into that city narrows.
where_we_lose.counter: Qualify the incumbent back office early. Where Passport is already in, lead with being the detection engine that feeds it rather than trying to displace the citation platform.

where_we_lose.headline: Payments, permits and enforcement on one contract
where_we_lose.detail: ParkMobile in 700-plus US cities, Passport in 800-plus, plus permits and pay stations. For a city that wants one vendor and one invoice, that is a strong procurement story we cannot match alone.
where_we_lose.counter: Separate the decisions. Insist enforcement detection is scoped and priced on its own, or it will not be properly evaluated.

where_we_lose.headline: Deep private-equity backing and a clear strategy
where_we_lose.detail: The Passport deal is backed by Vitruvian Partners, Verdane and Searchlight Capital Partners, and cleared a DOJ Second Request. Arrive is explicitly building a 'City OS' for curb management ahead of autonomous vehicle deployment.
where_we_lose.counter: Do not contest the strategy. Ask what is funded and shipping for detection specifically, and on what timeline.

where_we_lose.headline: In-car and consumer distribution
where_we_lose.detail: Parkopedia puts parking data and payments into automaker dashboards, and the group owns ParkMobile, EasyPark and RingGo outright. That is a driver relationship we have no equivalent for.
where_we_lose.counter: Not our market. Keep the conversation on detection quality and what the patrol returns.

landmines.question: Whose LPR hardware and engine are detecting the violation, and is that vendor contracted to you or to Arrive?
landmines.why: Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware, so there is a third party in the chain that the city may not be contracting with directly.

landmines.question: What is the evidence standard when a citation from that detection is contested, and who stands behind it in adjudication?
landmines.why: Separates citation workflow from evidence quality. The back office processes the citation; something else has to prove the violation.

landmines.question: Passport closed on 1 October 2026 and organisational structure updates are still to come. What has been committed on roadmap, pricing and support continuity?
landmines.why: Arrive's own completion release says structure updates will follow in the coming months.

landmines.question: Can the same enforcement patrol also return road-condition and asset data, or is that a separate procurement?
landmines.why: No Arrive brand publishes road-condition or asset-register detection.

landmines.question: Which Arrive are we contracting with? Flash still operates ParkWhiz and BestParking under the former Arrive Mobility name.
landmines.why: EasyPark bought the Arrive name from Flash in 2025; procurement records can confuse the two.

objections.objection: Arrive does enforcement now too, so why would we add you?
objections.response: They do, and Passport is a capable citation platform. Worth asking whose LPR is actually detecting the violation: Passport's own pages say it integrates with various LPR technologies and relies on third-party LPR hardware. We can be that engine, and feed their back office the way we feed gtechna today.

objections.objection: One vendor for payments, permits and enforcement is simpler for us.
objections.response: It is, if the bundle genuinely covers detection. Price the enforcement detection separately and ask for a reference city where the combined Arrive and Passport platform is issuing evidenced citations from its own detection. The deal completed on 1 October 2026, so that reference list is short.

objections.objection: We already use ParkMobile and now Passport. Switching is not on the table.
objections.response: Then do not switch. Keep both. We integrate as the detection layer into the citation system you already run, which is exactly how we work with gtechna in Pittsburgh, Kitchener and Medford.

objections.objection: Arrive is in 90 countries and has private-equity backing. You are much smaller.
objections.response: True on scale, and on payments they are formidable. On enforcement they bought the capability eight months ago and Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware, so ask who supplies the detection and how long that stack has been issuing evidenced citations together.

pricing_comparison.text: Neither side publishes municipal pricing. Arrive now offers payments, permits and enforcement on one contract across 800-plus North American cities through Passport, which is a bundling advantage rather than a published price advantage. SenSen is an annual subscription with no upfront capital expenditure. Where a city tenders payments and enforcement together, insist the detection scope is priced separately so it is actually evaluated rather than assumed to be covered.

proof_quotes.quote: Until now, Arrive has lacked a substantial compliance and enforcement offering in North America, a gap that Passport nicely fills.
Passport has declined to bid for or has lost some recent notable MPP contracts.

white_space.opportunity: Running detection on camera feeds the city already owns
white_space.evidence: SenDISA is sensor-agnostic and ingests the CCTV, GIS, sensor and traffic feeds a city already runs, alongside its own SenFORCE patrol cameras. AutoVu's ALPR runs on Genetec's own cameras, and Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware. All three vendors mount cameras on patrol vehicles, so the difference is what else the engine can read, not where the cameras sit.

white_space.opportunity: Multi-department value from a single patrol pass
white_space.evidence: No competitor in this set publishes road-condition, asset-register or kerb-inventory detection. Genetec's breadth is security; Arrive's is payments and mobility data.

white_space.opportunity: Being the detection engine inside someone else's citation platform
white_space.evidence: Passport, now owned by Arrive, relies on third-party LPR hardware, and gtechna already runs SenForce for Ticket-by-Mail. The detection layer is a separable, winnable component even where a rival owns the back office.

changes.change: Arrive completed its acquisition of Passport on 1 October 2026, adding parking compliance, citation issuance, digital permits and LPR-based enforcement across 800-plus North American cities. The DOJ closed its antitrust investigation on 8 October 2026.
changes.why_it_matters: Arrive is no longer a payments-only adjacency. It now owns the citation back office layer we partner into through gtechna.
changes.rep_action: Qualify the incumbent citation platform early, and position as the detection engine that feeds it rather than a replacement.

changes.change: EasyPark Group renamed itself Arrive on 12 June 2025, after buying the rights to the name from Flash, which had held them since its 2021 merger with the earlier Arrive Mobility (ParkWhiz and BestParking).
changes.why_it_matters: Two different US parking companies have traded under the name Arrive, and procurement records can confuse them.
changes.rep_action: Confirm which entity is being evaluated before comparing anything.

changes.change: Completed the acquisitions of Flowbird (January 2025) and Parkopedia (February 2025), then rebranded the group in June 2025.
changes.why_it_matters: Three major changes inside eighteen months is real integration load during a multi-year municipal contract.
changes.rep_action: Ask what has been committed on roadmap and support continuity post-integration.

changes.change: FY26: ARR A$11.7M up 17%, record cash receipts A$16.0M, EBITDA A$2.0M up 23.6%, churn 5.6%, but revenue only slightly ahead of the prior year after NVIDIA hardware supply delays pushed projects into FY27.
changes.why_it_matters: A prospect checking our numbers will see flat revenue; lead with ARR, EBITDA and churn and explain the supply-chain cause.
changes.rep_action: Quote 5.6% churn as the customer-churn number and never claim zero churn.

changes.change: Genetec's current fact sheet lists 2,300-plus employees, 42,500-plus clients and 159 countries, and in August 2026 Omdia and Novaira Insights ranked it the number one video management software vendor worldwide.
changes.why_it_matters: Scale and independently measured market leadership are their strongest cards in a risk-averse procurement.
changes.rep_action: Do not contest size. Move to scope: what the patrol returns beyond citations.

notes.Which Arrive this is: Arrive here is EasyPark Group, renamed on 12 June 2025 and parent of ParkMobile, EasyPark, Flowbird, RingGo, Parkopedia, Yellowbrick and YourParkingSpace. It is not Arrive Mobility, the ParkWhiz and BestParking business that merged into Flash in January 2021; EasyPark bought the rights to the name from Flash. In the United States the group trades mainly as ParkMobile, in over 700 cities.
notes.They are not all competing for the same: Genetec is a direct competitor for municipal enforcement: AutoVu is mobile and fixed ALPR plus vehicle investigation inside Security Center. Arrive became a competitor on 1 October 2026 when it completed the Passport acquisition, adding citation issuance, permits and LPR-based enforcement across 800-plus North American cities. Passport relies on third-party LPR hardware rather than supplying its own cameras, so Arrive competes for the back office and the bundle while the detection layer remains separable - and winnable.
notes.Buyer reviews: Rating and Market voice are deliberately unscored. Genetec Security Center is reviewed on G2, Gartner Peer Insights and Capterra at roughly 4 out of 5, but SenSen.ai has no buyer-review presence at all and Arrive's public ratings are consumer app-store scores for ParkMobile and EasyPark, which say nothing about how a city buyer rates the product. Scoring a category where only one of three vendors is rated would distort the leader badge, so it is left empty and the Genetec review signal is carried as prose instead.
notes.Where the accuracy figures are not compa: SenSen publishes over 98% ALPR accuracy and 99% accurate evidence packages, and those are self-reported. Genetec publishes no comparable accuracy figure. This card therefore makes no accuracy comparison and asks instead for contested-citation overturn rates on comparable deployments.
notes.Hosting claims: SenSen's IRAP Protected assessment and Sydney and Melbourne Azure hosting apply to Australian deployments. For United States deployments the company states regional Azure hosting, so no IRAP or US-specific accreditation is claimed in this report.
notes.Research method: Exa neural search over primary sources, then direct reading of ASX filings, Genetec's corporate fact sheet and press releases, Arrive, Passport and Flash announcements, the US Department of Justice antitrust statement, and trade press including Parking Today and Traffic Technology Today. An earlier draft of this report leaned too heavily on vendor websites and missed the Passport acquisition entirely; news, M&A and trade press for the last 12-18 months are now checked for every competitor before the card is finalised.
notes.Dated evidence: Genetec's Fort Lauderdale parking case study is undated and its embedded image metadata runs to 2015, so its payback and scofflaw figures are roughly a decade old and are labelled as such wherever they appear. Genetec's corporate fact sheet is dated July 2024; headcount and office figures here use the July 2025 expansion release and the February 2026 press summit instead.
notes.Arguments deliberately not used: SenSen's own SenFORCE cameras are vehicle-mounted, so no argument in this card criticises a competitor for running detection on patrol-vehicle cameras - it would apply equally to us. The sensor-agnostic fusion argument is used instead. SenSen's North American delivery also runs largely through channel partners, so this card makes no claim about contracting directly. Genetec's US headcount share was dropped as a weak argument against a company that sells through a 2,500-strong integrator network by design. The DOJ's finding about lost contracts is used only as a payments point, because that is what it covers.
notes.Founding dates: Published sources disagree on when SenSen was founded: 2007 is the most commonly cited year, with others suggesting 2005, and the ASX-listed entity arrived later through a back-door listing. 2007 is used here. Genetec's own material also disagrees with itself: the current fact sheet says 2,300-plus employees while the about page says 2,200-plus.
